item.title: Suburban women souring on Paxton could hurt him in tight Texas Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CYPRESS, Texas - There’s something missing in this conservative Houston suburb on the eve of early voting next Monday: Visible support for Republicans, particularly the embattled Senate candidate. In the sprawling Bridgeland subdivision, yard signs appear to favor Democratic state Rep. James Talarico over his rival, GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton. The signage gap matches recent polling, which shows Talarico, a four-term state representative, either tied or several points ahead of Paxton, who has never lost an election in 25 years. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Nowhere is that more clear than on Bridgeland’s Inspiration Drive, where voters on both sides of the political aisle say that Paxton, dogged by corruption scandals and accusations of infidelity, has lost support from a crucial segment of the electorate: suburban women. Interviews with these female voters, who tend to outvote men and therefore carry extra sway in growing communities, reveal a combination of apathy toward Paxton’s candidacy and an active shift by some conservatives toward his Democratic opponent. Republican Tess Eugenio, who works in human resources, said there is a split on her street between the vocal supporters for Talarico and those whom she suspects will vote for Paxton, even if they’re not advertising it. “People don’t want to talk about whether they’re going to vote for him, but they will,” Eugenio, 57, said of Paxton. “The question is, will it be enough?” Across the street, Maria Kostecka, a retired preschool teacher, said female friends and neighbors have approached her expressing enthusiasm for Talarico, especially after she posted his campaign yard sign. “I start to feel like it’s this secret underground club who don’t want Paxton in office,” said Kostecka, 66. She said she’s worried though that people “will stay home because they do not like the choices they have.” In a race that veteran political observers say will be decided by small margins, incremental shifts that eluded Democrats in recent cycles could be building in the suburbs. In 2022, Democratic Rep. Beto O’Rourke made gains in the suburbs, but in the end, Gov. Greg Abbott (R) still won 60 percent of suburban precincts to O’Rourke’s 38 percent, according to the Texas Politics Project. Unlike O’Rourke, polls have Talarico leading his GOP opponent by four to six points, and he’s far outpaced Paxton in direct fundraising, including a record-breaking $64 million in the third quarter compared to Paxton’s $18 million. Talarico leads even more among women: 56 percent of women said they would vote for Talarico, 40 percent for Paxton, according to a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released Tuesday. That margin exceeds the gap among all suburban voters, according to the same poll, which shows Talarico leading Paxton 54 to 44. Paxton recently received an infusion of $158 million in campaign funding via a Senate PAC from Texas-based tech billionaire Elon Musk, but he’s still saddled with President Donald Trump’s low approval ratings and his own checkered history. In 2023, Paxton was investigated and impeached in a bipartisan vote of the Texas House for bribery, abuse of official capacity and obstruction of justice. While Paxton was ultimately acquitted by the GOP-controlled state Senate, the trial detailed allegations Paxton had used his office to help a wealthy donor retaliate against whistleblowers and confess to staff that he’d cheated on his wife. Last year, a state judge in Houston dismissed a 2015 felony securities fraud case against Paxton after he completed a pretrial diversion program without admitting guilt. “He knows that gap exists and he’s trying to make it as small as possible,” Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University, said of Paxton’s support among women. “Republican primary voters made the decision to nominate the most deeply flawed Republican statewide candidate in modern history and that’s bearing fruit right now because Paxton has trouble winning anyone but the core Republican voters.” Like other conservative suburbs ringing Houston, Dallas and Austin, the Cypress-Fairbanks region has diversified during the past decade as it grew to nearly 700,000. It’s now 45 percent White, 25 percent Latino, 12 percent Asian and 12 percent Black, according to the latest census. In the 2018 midterm Senate election, O’Rourke won surrounding Harris County and made unprecedented gains in historically conservative suburban Fort Bend County to the south, flipping precincts in competitive congressional districts. He narrowed his margins in some western suburbs, but lagged in others including Cypress and ultimately lost to Sen. Ted Cruz (R). During the 2020 presidential race, some Cypress neighborhoods shifted 10 to 30 percentage points more Democratic compared to 2016, and Joe Biden won the county by 13 points. But no Democrat could pull off a statewide win. There are signs this year that could be changing. Even though 57 percent of the Cypress electorate has voted Republican and 43 percent Democrat, according to an analysis earlier this year, there has been a recent upswing in progressive activism. Control of the local MAGA-controlled school board flipped last year building support among independents. During the March primary, more Democrats voted than Republicans for the first time in four years in Harris County and statewide, driven in part by voting in the suburbs, experts said - and that could help decide the Senate race. “It’s an election of increments ... and the suburbs are where the voters are,” said James Henson, who leads the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, noting some of those votes are still in play. “There will be a lot of people who will make up their mind in the last weeks.” Last month, Paxton appeared at Glorious Way Church, which serves the Cypress area, to speak with supporters about the economy and his plans to lower costs for Texans, including tax deductions for medical expenses and first-time home buyers. “I’m going fight so every Texan can buy a home, raise a family and live a healthy life without struggling to make ends meet,” Paxton said, touting his “Protecting the Texas Promise” plan to address cost of living, housing and health care costs through tax relief and up-front pricing from hospitals and insurers. Talarico noted on X that when Paxton posted about the Cypress event, he misidentified the area as “Cyprus” - a European country - implying the error may have been due to Paxton’s “luxury European vacations.” Eugenio said she supports Paxton because she opposes gender transition care for minors, worries about child trafficking, border security and other public safety issues Paxton has championed. “Even though he has personal issues, that’s not my business,” she said. “I still feel like he would be a good fit.” Eugenio said she’d declined to be polled recently, and suspects other Paxton supporters have done the same, leading to undercounts. “There’s always the possibility that the polls are undercounting Republicans,” Jones, the political science professor, said. “Although even in that case the problem for Paxton is it’s probably only two or three points.” Paxton’s campaign appears to be attempting to solidify support among conservative and right-leaning suburban women with appeals by his family. He posted video speaking with his adult daughter about child-rearing. GOP state Sen. Angela Paxton, with whom he is embroiled in a contentious divorce, appeared in a campaign ad that did not name her husband but urged voters to support “the Republican ticket.” Such ads, Jones said, are “a rearguard attempt to stem the flow of women supporters and win back some of the conservative women who can’t bring themselves to vote for Ken Paxton.” “They’re potentially persuadable if you can soften the aspect of Paxton that has you believing he’s treated his wife and family poorly,” Jones said, so that they “revert to their traditional behavior and vote for the party.” Talarico has proposed an affordability plan he calls the “New American Dream” that includes, among other things, universal child care and down payment assistance for first-time home buyers. But Republican strategist Kristin Davison said many suburban voters remain unconvinced Democrats can address their affordability concerns. “Democrats are not offering a lot of what suburban women are looking at: How they are going to pay for soccer camp for two kids, keep their family budget intact,” she said. In Cypress, Nyna Saenz, 36, who leads a volunteer network canvassing for Talarico and other Democratic candidates, said it’s been contentious: “If you run into a die-hard Republican, they will slam the door in your face.” In her own family, she said she has conservative, religious relatives who plan to vote for Paxton, but at least one plans to abstain from voting due to Paxton’s infidelity (Angela Paxton’s divorce filing last year cited “biblical grounds and adultery.”) In Bridgeland, Maria Smith, a mother of two who works in medical content sales, said she fears that if Ken Paxton is elected, more corruption allegations will surface. Smith, 48, said she voted for Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary, but now plans to vote for Talarico because unlike Paxton, “he always answers questions directly.” Angela Paxton’s ad, she said, “was an even bigger turnoff.” “It’s ‘Do as I say, not as I do,’” she said, adding that she expects some conservative neighbors to stay home on Election Day. Watching her son’s flag-football game nearby, Michelle Burch described herself as independent: conservative on fiscal policy, liberal on social issues. Her husband, who like many in the area works in the oil and gas industry, plans to vote for Ken Paxton for economic reasons. But Burch, 42, an elementary schoolteacher, said she was voting based on the candidate’s character. “I’m teaching kids here’s what you do, here’s what you don’t do. And Paxton is not someone you can look up to,” she said. She mentioned Paxton’s theft of a pen from a courthouse, caught in security video, that Talarico highlighted in a campaign ad. “How you treat people should matter,” Burch said, describing Paxton as “not trustworthy.” A few streets over, McKenna Nevers, an independent fiscal conservative who didn’t vote in the primary, said she’s still undecided. Nevers, 39, a data consultant, said she was bothered by Paxton’s “smear campaign,” including a flier opposing gender transition care that she was afraid her two young children might see. Nevers, whose husband is a doctor, said parents should make decisions about care for transgender children in consultation with their doctors, particularly on hormones children might need for other reasons. And Nevers said that’s not the main concern deciding her vote. “Maybe because I’m a mom, it’s: What’s your position on how you’re going to make our life better?” she said. She said Talarico promised to address issues that concern her - public schools, safety, affordability, taxes. But she wasn’t sure he could work across the aisle to get results in Washington. “I generally like the way that he talks, but that doesn’t mean I’m going to vote for him,” Nevers said. “Can he get what he’s talking about done?” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/10/19/suburban-women-souring-paxton-could-doom-him-tight-race/

item.title: Democrats may have an unlikely ally in a post-midterms effort to oust Hegseth
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Senate Democrats are quietly floating the ouster of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth after the Nov. 3 election as the political price for cooperation on key defense-related issues in the postelection lame-duck session, and they may have some GOP support to shake up the Pentagon’s leadership, according to Senate sources. The Defense Department has set recruiting records under Hegseth’s leadership, and the Pentagon chief appears to have strong support from President Trump, who likes to brag that Hegseth looks like a military leader from “central casting.” But some Republican senators haven’t been happy with Hegseth’s leadership, especially his ouster of well-respected military leaders such as Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, Army chief of staff Randy George, Navy Secretary John Phelan and four-star Gen. Chris Donahue, the top U.S. military officer in Europe. Democrats view Hegseth’s leadership as a disaster and are looking for leverage to push him out after the midterm elections, according to Senate sources, just as they attempted to push former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem out of her job during the prolonged stalemate over funding for her department earlier this year. Trump eventually fired Noem after key Republican senators, such as Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), turned against her publicly. Now Democrats have significant leverage over Hegseth’s future at the Pentagon as they’re threatening to hold up emergency defense funding the White House requested in June as well as regular funding for the Defense Department, which expires on Dec. 11. Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hegseth’s resignation could set the stage for more bipartisan cooperation on must-pass defense bills, such as the National Defense Authorization Act and the annual defense appropriations bill. Kaine told The Hill before the Senate adjourned for the election that Hegseth’s departure would help lower the partisan temperature in the standoff over the defense measures. Republican sources say that Senate Democrats have already privately floated Hegseth’s termination as something that could help muster bipartisan cooperation on filling key vacancies at the Pentagon, such as the positions of Army and Navy secretary left open by the departures of Driscoll and Phelan. As things now stand, Senate Democrats are threatening to block the defense spending bills and also a waiver for Hung Cao, Trump’s nominee to serve as Navy secretary. Cao needs a special congressional waiver to lead the Navy because federal law requires a seven-year waiting period before former military officers can be confirmed to top Pentagon civilian leadership posts. Democrats are drawing a hard line on supporting defense funding in the lame-duck session if the military conflict with Iran isn’t wrapped up before the end of the year. “My own view is that if the war is over, then the opportunity for bipartisanship on defense authorization and defense appropriations is there. I think if the war’s not over, it’s going to be extremely difficult,” said Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is poised to take over as Democratic whip in the next Congress. Schatz said he was speaking about his personal view of the prospects of a deal on defense spending. So far, some key Senate Republicans say they don’t see Trump agreeing to push Hegseth out of the job to get cooperation from Democrats on the defense authorization and funding measures in the lame-duck session. “That’s a bridge too far,” warned a GOP senator, who requested anonymity to discuss the looming negotiations over breaking the logjam on defense legislation after Election Day. A senior Pentagon official dismissed the criticism of Hegseth’s leadership from Democrats and some key Republicans by pointing to his record of accomplishments over the past 20 months. “Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength,” the official said in response to jockeying by Democrats to push Hegseth out of his role, using the Trump administration's preferred name for the Department of Defense. “Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs. Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before,” the senior official said. “The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” There are growing questions, however, on Capitol Hill about whether Trump and Hegseth are fully in sync on several important issues. Trump recently cancelled Hegseth’s plan to run a livestream of the execution of Maj. Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 at a mass shooting at Fort Hood in 2009. There’s also confusion about whether Hegseth or other senior Pentagon officials directed a temporary halt to intelligence sharing with Ukraine or ordered the restriction of Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite-based internet network, without Trump’s knowledge and approval. Four Republican senators — Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (Maine), Sen. John Cornyn (Texas), Sen. Thom Tillis (N.C.) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) — signed a bipartisan letter last week directing the Defense Department inspector general, Platte Moring, demanding he immediately investigate whether any Pentagon officials “directed” or “authorized” changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine. Collins has separately faulted Hegseth for not fully anticipating that Iran would be able to shut down most shipping traffic, including nearly a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil supply, through the vulnerable Strait of Hormuz in response to U.S. and Israeli attacks. “For example, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz should have been anticipated. It happened during the Iraq-Iran war and it’s an obvious point of leverage but there doesn’t seem to have been any plan for it,” Collins said last month. Tillis wrote in his new memoir that his decision to cast a deciding vote to confirm Hegseth in January 2025 is “the biggest regret of my career.” Some Republicans already acknowledge that pushing Hegseth out of his job in the lame-duck session could avoid a messy impeachment battle next year, aside from paving the way for a potential deal on the defense authorization and appropriations bills before Christmas. “Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth’s impeachment. It’s the honorable thing to do,” Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) posted Thursday on the social platform X. The maverick conservative who lost his primary reelection bid earlier this year when Trump endorsed his opponent noted that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) had to scramble to avoid voting on Hegseth’s impeachment before the election. “The House recessed early to avoid the vote, so I will reintroduce Hegseth articles of impeachment when we return for the lame duck session, regardless of the outcome of the midterm election,” House Democrats, led by Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April. Democrats in the lower chamber plan to make Hegseth a top political target next year if they win the majority in next month’s election, something that political handicappers project is likely. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) told Semafor that impeaching Hegseth should be one of House Democrats’ “top three priorities” next year. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: Iran threatens to target AI centers and undersea cables if war with U.S. resumes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Iranian Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi speaks during a press conference in Tehran, Iran, on September 29. - Majid Asgaripour/Wana News Agency/Reuters Iran has signaled that it is preparing for another round of war with the United States and has issued public threats against Washington and its allies in an apparent bid to deter President Donald Trump from restarting the current conflict. Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built large stockpiles of new weapons ready to be unleashed on targets beyond the region should the US resume hostilities that began in February. Iranian officials have threatened to broaden their targets if the conflict resumes, floating options that include cutting undersea internet cables, striking AI data centers, and attacking regional oil and gas facilities. “The world will be amazed,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said late last month. “We have new targets that have not yet been attacked,” he added. Nearly nine months after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran , the conflict has stagnated into a stalemate that has left everyone uncertain about Trump’s endgame and the world grappling with economic unrest. Both sides have claimed victory – Tehran pointing to its survival and Washington the damage inflicted on the Iranian regime. Meanwhile, the Trump administration continues testing new economic and military measures to force Iran into capitulation, which Tehran has stubbornly resisted. “The war is not over,” Mohebbi said. “The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has prepared itself for a long-term war.” Bracing for war While Iran’s commanders signal strength and readiness, ordinary Iranians, long burdened by conflict and economic uncertainty, are once again bracing for the on the ground realities of war. “Every single day and every night, we’re waiting for the bombing to start again,” a 70-year-old Tehran resident told CNN last week. “I’ve charged all my power banks, stocked up on water, and got everything ready, because the attacks could start again at any moment, any day.” A mother of two described to CNN the fear she lives with as she sends her children to school each morning, past streets where Revolutionary Guards are visible, and military bases remain active. “I would like to know exactly what else the US is planning to bomb?” she said. “They couldn’t even take (the Iranian leadership) out. You couldn’t negotiate either. So, what’s the point of starting another war?” A plume of smoke rises following a missile strike on a building in Tehran on March 1. - Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images Iranians are “convinced” war is going to restart, another resident in Tehran told CNN. “It’s all anyone can talk about…you just have it in the back of your head, is tonight the night? Is it tomorrow? I think it makes it worse that there areall this conversation about it, you can’t even take a break,” the resident told CNN. The Iranians spoke to CNN on the condition of anonymity in order to speak freely about their fears of further war. Targeting Europe Over the last few weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterm elections, several advisers told CNN privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before election day on November 3. The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter. The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal and would mark a notable escalation. “These are propaganda tools intended to intimidate the Iranian people,” Alireza Sheikh, an Iranian army commander said on Saturday. “The Iranian people are the father of all bombs.” Iran has signaled a new, more offensive military doctrine that suggests it will not wait to be struck and could even launch pre-emptive strikes. Last week, Revolutionary Guards social media accounts reported that Iran conducted military exercises across the country, including launching 30 ballistic missiles in one go. Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with The Washington Institute think tank focused on US foreign policy in the region, said if an emboldened Tehran decided to try its new long-range missiles against Europe in an attack, targets might include US forces based at airbases in England, or the logistic hub in Ramstein, Germany, the largest US military installation outside of the US. “However, Iran would likely reserve that possibility to a very top level of escalation,” Nadimi said. The US moved all of its long-range bombers stationed in the United Kingdom back to their American home bases earlier this month after an unspecified new threat, officials said. Days before the move, the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the US bombers had been stationed. B‑1B Lancer bomber at the UK's RAF Fairford airbase, which hosts US Air Force personnel. - Toby Shepheard/Reuters Armed police stand guard manning a roadblock at an entrance to RAF Fairford base in Fairford, south-west England. - Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images To increase their chances of hitting targets, Nadimi said Iran may potentially launch more sophisticated and coordinated swarms of AI-enabled drones fitted with cameras and datalinks that can communicate with each other, adjust flight paths and speed to evade jamming and air defenses. “They haven’t demonstrated these capabilities yet, but they discussed developing such technologies in the past,” Nadimi said. Iran may also seek to advance its cruise missile capabilities to include supersonic propulsion to better evade interception and try jamming military communication and surveillance satellites, he added. Region prepared Iranian commanders are preparing for what they regard as an inevitable resumption in hostilities, while also attempting to deter Washington by highlighting the costs of an attack, Ali Vaez, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at International Crisis Group told CNN. “Tehran wants to make clear that the next round will be fought on a much wider battlefield, with fewer restraints and potentially more lethal consequences,” Vaez said. “But the danger is that what Iran intends as deterrence could be interpreted in Washington as provocation, making the very war Tehran hopes to avert more likely.” When the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, they killed the Islamic Republic’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei along with Iranian military commanders, top officials, and civilians, including schoolchildren. Iran’s retaliation focused mostly on its Arab neighbors, which it accuses of colluding with Washington. Iran effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, the only maritime waterway used by neighboring nations to export oil, before striking civilian infrastructure across Arab cities. Dubai, a major tourist destination, was targeted, water plants in Kuwait were hit, and attacks on data centers disrupted banking services in several countries across the region. An aerial view shows ships anchored off the coast of Khasab in Oman's Musandam Governorate, near the Strait of Hormuz, on October 2. - AFP/Getty Images Iran fired more than 2,500 missiles and drones on the United Arab Emirates alone, more than any other country, including Israel. Abu Dhabi intercepted nearly all of the projectiles, according to figures by the UAE’s defense ministry. Last week, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, warned that Iran will target US assets in the region, including within the UAE, in retaliation for any fresh attacks “If another war breaks out, numerous undersea cables, data centers, AI facilities and other infrastructure across the region could be destroyed,” Rezaei said. A senior UAE official told journalists on Thursday that his country is better prepared should fighting resume. “We don’t want war,” Ali Al-Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE’s Federal National Council said. “But if a war starts today, we are ready to deal with any threat that comes our way better than we were on February 28.” “Whatever is needed to protect our national security, sovereignty and people, we will do it.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/19/middleeast/iran-us-conflict-warning-intl

item.title: France imposes curfews after violent protests lead to thousands of arrests
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Sudip Kar-Gupta and Elizabeth Pineau PARIS, Oct 19 (Reuters) - French authorities set curfews in parts of several cities on Monday, including Paris, Lille and Nice, as they faced pressure over security failings after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu had ruled out a blanket curfew in Paris but not a state of emergency, and had said ‌it was more appropriate for now to apply partial and localised curfews. "My determination to restore order is absolute," he told reporters. Paris police said they had issued orders barring protests in certain areas of ‌the French capital from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) and had issued a curfew around the Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11:00 p.m. Both would remain in effect until 6 a.m. on Tuesday morning. "A police deployment is in place to ensure strict compliance with these measures," ​the police said in a statement. A source in Lecornu's office said a curfew for minors had been set between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. for the next two days in Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain with the agreement of the local mayors. In Nice, mayor Eric Ciotti said in a video posted online that he had signed an order installing a curfew for minors in central Nice overnight. Marseille banned gatherings and demonstrations. French unions meanwhile called for a new round of strikes and rallies on November 5. The weekend of looting and violence between some protesters and police followed weeks of student demonstrations, rocking France six months ahead of its next presidential election and highlighting pressures from a weak economy and surging debt. MINISTER ‌BLAMES FAR LEFT Lecornu blamed far-left groups for some of France's worst unrest in ⁠years. "There is, after all, a far-left movement that wants to cause — we can’t put it any more strongly — profound unrest in the country in the run-up to the presidential election," he said. Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon urged him to provide evidence. "Otherwise, he should apologise, keep quiet and stop fanning the flames of unrest," he said on X. The Federation of Trade ⁠and Retail said almost 3,000 shops had been affected over the weekend. "Behind every ransacked shop are business owners, employees and families who have seen years of work and effort wiped out in a matter of hours," it added, calling for social security and tax relief for affected businesses. Lecornu said the government would provide furlough measures from Tuesday. Standing before a boarded-up shopfront, Gerard Nouchi, manager of two clothing stores in Marseille, said there weren't enough police to stop the looters. "They trashed everything, broke things, insulted ​us,” ​Nouchi said. "It was like a real tornado." The government ordered platforms selling looted goods to take down announcements and collaborate to prosecute ​resellers, Junior Digital Minister Anne Le Hénanff wrote on X. Some 2,400 people were arrested and ‌one protester died from a cardiac arrest on Saturday while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the Interior Ministry. 'LEFT WITHOUT PROTECTION' French assets were underperforming broader European markets on Monday, though moves were more contained than at some other moments of recent political friction. Tensions in President Emmanuel Macron's fragile government over apparent security shortcomings — coming as the government needs to pass a budget bill to rein in its finances — could further unsettle investors. Macron's office said on Monday he had turned down his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez's offer to resign, telling him instead to put an end to barricades and looting and be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings". Nunez told reporters that Tuesday evening's Champions League soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona would go ahead as planned. The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon said in a joint op-ed in the newspaper Liberation that they were used to demonstrations and protests. "But on Saturday ... ‌for the first time, we had the feeling that whole sections of our cities had been left without protection," said the ​mayors, all from the centre-left. The start of school holidays on Monday may provide relief, but students were staging more gatherings and blockades in some places, ​including the Louvre gallery and Sciences Po university in central Paris. LUXURY BOUTIQUES DAMAGED At the weekend, hundreds of thousands ​took to the streets to protest over what many say are declining and dysfunctional public services. At the Place Vendome in Paris, home to luxury hotels and boutiques, most shops were shuttered ‌and surrounded by security guards on Monday. The front door of a Dior boutique was ​smashed, while windows belonging to other luxury brand stores in ​central Paris, including Rolex, Louis Vuitton, Ralph Lauren and Gucci, were damaged. In Marseille, Ligue 1 club Olympique de Marseille said its official store on the city's historic main avenue had been looted, while a town hall in central France was torched. France deployed 60,000 police and other security forces on Saturday, Nunez told France Inter radio, but he acknowledged that was not enough to control violent crowds. Cost-of-living issues also drove ​weekend protests in other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania. European governments have ‌advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution. As France was busy cleaning up its streets, Macron arrived in Kuwait for a Gulf trip aimed at securing additional petrol ​and diesel supplies to bring down pump prices. (Reporting by Zhifan Liu, Tassilo Hummel, Elizabeth Pineau, Dominique Vidalon, Alessandro Parodi and Makini Brice in Paris, Sudip Kar-Gupta in Brussels, Amanda Cooper, Alun John ​and Helen Reid in London; Writing by Tassilo Hummel and Charlie Devereux; Editing by Aidan Lewis and Andrew Cawthorne) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/frances-macron-declines-interior-ministers-052023968.html

item.title: West Virginia officials offered to store nuclear waste. Then residents found out.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
HARPERS FERRY, W.Va. - The jagged limestone rocks of Old Standard Quarry have weathered many eras of history. The property was the site of a Civil War battle, then a quarry and is now a popular destination for bungee jumping, its dark green water fed by a natural spring. Recently, the state proposed yet another use for the land: as storage for radioactive nuclear waste from around the country. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “I thought it was a joke,” said Pasha Majdi, president of the Jefferson County Commission. “It doesn’t make any sense.” It wasn’t a joke. Without consulting residents or local officials, Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s energy office submitted a detailed pitch to the Trump administration offering the Jefferson County quarry and three other sites for a potential “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.” The Trump administration has said such campuses would need to agree to store spent nuclear fuel - one of the nation’s most vexing environmental problems - in exchange for federal support for research, development and production facilities that aim to modernize and grow the country’s nuclear power infrastructure. The administration claims the campuses could create 25,000 jobs and generate tens of billions of dollars in private investment and tax revenue. Those economics are alluring to states eager for development. Twenty-six expressed some manner of interest before the federal government chose Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Idaho and West Virginia as finalists. “West Virginia is intentionally beginning with nuclear initiatives that are actionable and high‑value, particularly those tied to the spent and partially spent fuel stream and backend services, areas where the state can quickly demonstrate success and build momentum,” the state’s pitch promised. It assured that “West Virginia recognizes that for any project with potential community impacts, social buy-in and community alignment are foundational.” But the way things played out in West Virginia underscored how community anxiety around nuclear waste is not easily overcome. That anxiety is why there is no comprehensive plan for permanently disposing of the tens of thousands of tons of spent fuel that already exists in the United States, much less for getting rid of the waste that could be generated with the quadrupling of nuclear power capacity President Donald Trump envisions. As soon as details of the West Virginia proposal were disclosed, thanks to a public records request by the Charleston Gazette-Mail, the backlash was intense. Days after dismissing the report as “fake news,” Morrisey (R) withdrew the state from consideration altogether. The Morrisey administration did not respond to requests for comment. Energy Department spokesman Ben Dietderich said in an emailed statement that “the program has proven to be a huge success - with more than 25 states applying to participate - much of that success can be attributed [to] allowing states and local communities decide for themselves if an innovation campus is right for them.” The West Virginia episode, though, left communities bewildered, the governor politically wounded and the nuclear waste problem unresolved. The nuclear life cycle campus competition comes after the federal government tried - and failed - to create a repository for spent fuel for decades. Congress had designated Yucca Mountain, Nevada, as the most suitable place for it. But local opposition derailed that plan. Now, the focus is on finding a “consent-based” solution that would be developed in coordination with communities interested in developing facilities. Such a model has been successful in parts of Europe. It typically takes many years of deliberation and negotiation by the communities involved. “I’m personally a bit skeptical that states are going to move as fast as the [Trump] administration wants or is expecting,” said Matt Bowen, a nuclear scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy who has been tracking the life cycle campus initiative. The difficult conversations state officials need to have with the cities and counties that would host nuclear campuses are just getting underway. Nuclear industry officials say states taking a deliberative, democratic approach are getting genuine interest from communities that are viable candidates for a campus. In West Virginia, though, state officials appear not to have communicated with each other or the towns they were offering up in their pitch. And their experience shows how quickly the process can go sideways. Far from the fast-growing Harpers Ferry region, in economically struggling Boone County, the state’s nuclear pitch called for storing waste at what was once one of the largest mountaintop-removal coal mines in the country - an environmentally damaged site the state and local community have for years been seeking to convert into a redevelopment opportunity. The former coal-mining stronghold has lost nearly one-fifth of its population since 2010, as jobs disappeared. But the nuclear campus proposal landed with a thud there, too. Local opposition quickly emerged. The area’s state representative expressed frustration on social media that the community had not been consulted and relief when the state scrapped the proposal. The proposal had highlighted the potential benefits of a new state law, written for data center developers, that allows for fast-track approval of permits while bypassing local governments. “It felt for many of us like: ‘Here we go again,’” said Christine Wimer, president of the Jefferson County Foundation, a conservation advocacy group. “This is the same old thing in West Virginia. People come here. They get the good stuff. We get taken advantage of.’” Wimer said everything about the site the state was proposing near Harpers Ferry was unworkable. The porous limestone is particularly ill-suited for storing toxic materials. Half the property is a federally protected conservation zone, forever honoring its status as a historic battlefield. The other half, she said, is underwater. “Limestone essentially works like a highway for waste,” said Cara Keys, a county commissioner, as she stood over the quarry. “You could put something here, and it could infect someone’s well 20 miles away. The fact that they thought this could be a nuclear waste dump is very concerning.” Steve Pearson, editor of Jefferson County’s Observer Weekly newspaper, dove deep into the details of the proposal and emerged perplexed how it ever got submitted. “Even if you just wanted to build a warehouse, you could not do it there,” he said. “There is no land for it.” Down the road from the quarry in Middleway, a remarkably well-preserved village of 18th- and 19th-century stone, brick and log buildings on the National Register of Historic Places, farmers were already exhausted trying to stop plans for a large water-bottling plant that developers are seeking to build over the vociferous objections of community leaders, who warn it would be an environmental mess. The news that the state hoped to store nuclear waste nearby left them stunned. “I like to be left alone,” said David Liskey, 75, who has been in the area all his life. His ancestors started farming there in the mid-1700s. “People like it here the way it is. We don’t want what they are talking about doing.” Gabby Wilson has only been in the area a short time, having recently relocated from North Carolina. But Wilson, the owner of Prismatic Art Studio in downtown Charles Town, was every bit as blunt as Liskey. “It’s just gross,” she said of the nuclear campus proposal. “We moved here to get away from things like that.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/19/how-pitch-store-nuclear-waste-by-historic-battlefield-fell-apart/

item.title: Republicans already know who they want to blame if they suffer big midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans are already starting to blame each other as the midterm election spirals further out of their control. Everyone is bracing for President Donald Trump's ire if the party loses big in November. House Republicans are planning to accuse the Senate side. Trump political aides have taken to directly calling campaigns they feel aren't performing well enough. National GOP operatives are quietly furious at lackluster candidates who didn't do enough to prepare for a tough year despite early warnings. And some GOP candidates are pointing the finger back at their own party committees. It's a vicious cycle, according to more than a dozen top GOP operatives and lawmakers who spoke to POLITICO, some of whom were granted anonymity to candidly discuss private conversations. “If it happens, there will be plenty of blame to go around,” said Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-N.J.), who is in his own tighter-than-comfortable race. That Republicans have already spent significant time gaming out the aftermath and how to insulate themselves from the fallout of what they fear will be significant GOP losses illustrates how precarious the current landscape is for the party. That’s even as top Republicans publicly insist they are bullish on keeping control of both chambers in Congress. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who is widely expected to be the next National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, told reporters Thursday that “if the Democrats do win the House and the Senate, it won't be because of their left-wing lunatic candidates, it'll be because people are pissed off about gas prices, and I get that.” House Republicans are annoyed with Senate Republicans for fumbling a once-safe GOP map as well as creating top-of-the-ticket drag for them with bad candidates in some key states — but senators privately put the onus on Trump for forcing out better Republican incumbents and then backing flawed GOP candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas , according to three GOP senators and a national GOP operative. The top Senate GOP Super PAC and Trump’s MAGA Inc. have spent nearly $200 million alone to save Paxton, who’s locked in a tight race with Democrat James Talarico. Trump, for his part, has already landed on who to blame in the event of a Paxton loss next month. “If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday afternoon , targeting the Texas senator he endorsed against in the primary in Cornyn, and a longtime GOP foe in Rove. There’s also particular frustration with Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who numerous GOP operatives grumbled never took his race seriously and is now costing the party millions of dollars to rescue in a state Democrats haven’t won in almost a century. Marshall’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. “No one in the world expected that the Senate would need as much money as they did,” said one national GOP operative working on multiple competitive House races. “All of this money that was expected to go to the House, for the most part, is now being wasted on the Senate because they fucked up so bad.” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle blasted “armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation” and said Trump “is laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress this November, which is why he is traveling across the country highlighting the historic victories his Administration has delivered for the American people.” “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction,” Ingle said. “Those who are actually involved with Republicans' midterm strategy remain laser-focused on winning races and are confident we are still in a position to protect and expand our majorities," said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. A slew of troubling internal GOP polling in recent weeks set off a new level of panic across House GOP leadership, political operations and individual campaigns. It didn’t just reveal a harsh environment for the party in power on par with typical midterms, but potentially catastrophic scenarios in formerly safe red seats across the country. Even top House Republicans expect to lose the House majority at this point. A growing group of Hill Republicans argue the blame rests with Trump, and his decisions to get the U.S. into an open-ended war with Iran that has driven up fuel prices, while enacting a slew of tariffs and other policy moves that have riled farmers. “I’ve talked to some who are making these decisions: The biggest problem is the president’s polling numbers and unfavorables,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) recently told POLITICO . Still, not everyone is blaming Trump: In an explosive move this week, GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, who is close with the president and faces her own surprisingly competitive race, accused the National Republican Congressional Committee of dropping the ball. “I am also getting calls from members wondering what is going on at the @NRCC,” Luna posted on social media , adding she was also getting inquiries about House leadership races. “Sounds to me like some in leadership need to focus on winning races instead of gaming their next steak donor dinner.” (The post has since been deleted.) Some rank-and-file Republicans are frustrated the NRCC didn’t pivot faster to trying to shore up at-risk GOP incumbents across the map as the landscape deteriorated in August and September. “The leadership at the NRCC is living in a bubble,” another House Republican said. “We’re getting killed out here.” Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the NRCC, noted that the committee moved early to launch coordinated advertising campaigns with incumbents in districts not initially rated as competitive, including those represented by Reps. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.), Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.), Rob Wittman (R-Va.), Mike Turner (R-Ohio), and Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas). To date, the NRCC has run coordinated advertising in 51 districts, Marinella said. GOP lawmakers and operatives working to defend the party’s majorities in Congress have been discussing amongst themselves how to avoid being thrown under the bus come Nov. 3, according to a dozen of the people interviewed. The rising tensions have also turned up in the rather intense shadow leadership race underway within Speaker Mike Johnson’s circle and the senior ranks of the House GOP, with opposing camps preparing to blame each other, according to five of the people. GOP Whip Tom Emmer has said publicly that some of the GOP redistricting efforts won’t work, and Republicans won’t win all those seats. Trump officials have also been feeling the pressure, sometimes calling campaigns to try to revive lagging operations or attempting to install new staff within them, according to two Republicans familiar with the matter. In another stunning move, Trump officials are warning Republicans that pro-Trump super PACs can only help so much and the candidates need to shift their strategy to a positive message and a list of key deliverables for voters — or they will lose. “Republican success in many cases is going to hinge on the following: do they give voters a reason to vote for them?” a senior Republican official familiar with MAGA Inc.’s plans said. “They're being inundated with reasons to vote against the Democrats, and in many places they already instinctually want to. But are they given a reason to actually vote for the Republicans to show up and vote?” The person added that “the number one thing that every Republican in the country” should be doing in the final weeks is laying out “things that they are going to do to tangibly improve people's personal economic situation and their life” and “lower your cost of living.” “If Republicans are failing to lay out a reason to come vote for them and saying, ‘Here's what I, as a candidate, am for, what I am going to do to make your economics better,’ there’s a good chance they're going to lose,” the Republican official warned. That assessment has shocked several Republicans in tough races. It’s a big shift from even how House leadership has approached the campaign trail: Johnson has spent the last few weeks hammering a message of contrast between his party of “common sense” and Democrats as a party of dangerous socialists who will investigate the president and empower America’s “enemies” if they win. “We’re running for our lives,” another House Republican in a tough race said. “Those are two totally different approaches. And we have two weeks.” Erin Doherty contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/republican-knives-out-midterms-trump-01124859

item.title: Mission set to blast off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The spacecraft will head to Mars's larger moon, Phobos [JAXA] A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth. If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027. It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed. Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. "I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said. [BBC] There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos. Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes. The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos. It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat. Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon. "The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained. "But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface." Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formed [NASA] The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos. Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust. This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia. The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g. "It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission. "However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said. The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of Phobos [JAXA] Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from. There are two competing ideas. Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris. Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity. "When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell. "It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly." The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs. "One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell. "And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars." Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum [Kevin Church/BBC News] Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists. The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters. But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress. China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031. We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites. These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth. Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water. Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine. item.title: Mass. GOP candidate for lieutenant governor suspends campaign after arrest
item.description:

The former Massachusetts lieutenant governor-hopeful who was arrested in connection with drunken driving on Saturday night appeared in New Bedford court on Monday morning. Shawn Oliver, 42, is facing charges of operating under the influence (OUI) of alcohol in addition to motor vehicles charges of negligent operation, marked lanes violation and speeding, according to charging documents in his case. Oliver pleaded not guilty and was ordered released on personal recognizance from New Bedford District Court on Monday morning by Judge Joseph Harrington Jr. He is scheduled to appear again on Nov. 16. Oliver is a current New Bedford city councilor and Bristol County House of Corrections officer who was running on the ticket as a Republican candidate with Mike Minogue against current Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll and Gov. Maura Healey. He announced he was suspending his campaign at around 2 p.m. on Sunday, less than 24 hours after his arrest Saturday night and after Minogue had called on him to do so Sunday morning. Read more: The Mass. GOP’s lieutenant governor candidate suspended his campaign. Here’s what’s next “After careful reflection, I have made the decision to suspend my campaign for Lieutenant Governor,” Oliver, who was running as a Republican in the race, said in a statement released at 2:17 p.m. on Sunday. “This election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters. I want to sincerely thank everyone who has supported me throughout this journey and ask that my family’s privacy be respected during this difficult time,” Oliver said. Oliver’s attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Monday. What happened? According to three New Bedford police reports on the incident, Oliver was driving a black Lincoln Navigator north on Dartmouth Street at around 11:30 p.m., just south of the Rockdale Avenue intersection. A witness who spoke to officers at the scene said he was stopped in his own car behind Oliver’s Navigator at an intersection light on Dartmouth Street. When the light turned green, the witness said the Navigator did not pull forward. After a few moments sitting at the light — and the witness reversing his own car to view that the light was green — the Navigator suddenly accelerated forward and drifted to the right, almost hitting the curb by New York Bagel at 571 Dartmouth St., the report read. The Navigator then “abruptly” veered to the left to avoid striking the curb, the report read, and continued onward. After crossing through the Dartmouth and Rockdale intersection, the Navigator again drifted to the left and crossed over the yellow center line. Police say Oliver struck five parked cars and was driving so fast that he flipped his Navigator upside down onto its roof. Oliver was outside of the car and standing on the sidewalk, speaking on his cellphone when officers arrived at the scene, the report read. A bystander brought out a chair and officers told Oliver to sit down, noting that he was bleeding from an injury on the right side of his head. Oliver repeatedly asked officers at the scene if “everyone else was OK,” though they told him he was the only person involved in the crash, the report read. item.title: Justice Dept. is suing 30 states over voter data. Even Republicans are pushing back.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
With midterm elections just two weeks away, there are concerns that the federal government's pressure on election officials is breeding distrust in the system. Federal agents have seized ballots , and voting machines have been examined. The Justice Department is locked in legal battles with states across the country over information about individual voters and this past week threatened to prosecute California election officials if they knowingly count mail-in ballots from 20,000 people the Trump administration says are "likely noncitizens." It's a kind of interference Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, a Republican in a deeply red state, said she's never seen before. "In the past two elections that I oversaw as lieutenant governor, the threats were all external: non-state actors, cyber security threats and other things," she said. "But now we also have threats coming from within our own government." Federal government actions on elections In the U.S., elections are local. They're run by towns and counties and states. It's stated in Article I of the Constitution. Congress makes laws regulating elections, but the president doesn't have a role in running them. Still, during his second term Mr. Trump has signed two executive orders around voting: one requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and another on mail-in ballots . The administration's latest move came Thursday, when the Justice Department sued California , claiming it was mailing ballots to more than 20,000 likely noncitizens. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said the federal government was threatening the right of thousands of Californians to vote without providing any detail about how they identified those individuals, and she questioned the accuracy of the data. The Justice Department's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber said in a statement . "Noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections," head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon told 60 Minutes. "So the question is simply how many of them there are." Demands for voter rolls Last year the Justice Department asked nearly every state in the country for their full and complete voter rolls, including confidential voter information. "They wanted things that we typically are required by law to keep private: social security numbers, full dates of birth, driver's license numbers," said Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, who is responsible for Utah's elections. Henderson told 60 Minutes she wasn't given good answers about why the federal government wanted the information, and she was concerned about what would be done with the data. She refused to turn them over. Officials in 29 other states — Democratic and Republican — have also refused to comply with the government's demands. The Justice Department has sued all of them. The Trump administration says access to voter rolls will help purge the lists of immigrant voters who are not entitled to vote. The administration has alleged, without providing evidence, that 278,000 noncitizens are registered to vote. And a White House spokesperson has said that noncitizens "continue to register and vote in federal elections." Noncitizen voting does happen, but it's extremely rare. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said this summer that thousands of noncitizens were mistakenly registered in her state due to a software glitch. About 340 of them actually voted. Since the beginning of Mr. Trump's second term, the Justice Department has charged more than 100 noncitizens with voting illegally. Henderson said she found just 52 questionable voters on the rolls out of more than 2 million registered voters in Utah. DHS Secretary Mullin this summer said that any election official who knowingly allows noncitizens to vote could be prosecuted, or even sent to prison." "We're not going to prison. No. It's silly," Henderson said. Last month, in writing, the Justice Department told Henderson she was under investigation. "I have to tell myself it doesn't matter what the consequences are, as long as I feel like I'm doing what's right," she said. "I think this is an important thing for me to do, holding these guard rails, holding the line. Someone has to." Henderson believes there can still be honest and fair elections. The question for her is whether the losing candidate will accept the results. "We are seeing a trend of candidates who lose races now refusing to concede, saying it was rigged, saying it wasn't fair, even when it isn't close," she said. "Candidates who lose can do so much good by graciously conceding. That will instill confidence in the public." "I never imagined that we would be raided by the FBI" In January, armed federal agents seized ballots from a local facility in Fulton County, Georgia. "In my wildest dreams, I never imagined that we would be raided by the FBI," Fulton County Commissioner Dana Barrett, a Democrat, told 60 Minutes. The agents had a criminal search warrant that Georgia's secretary of state described as being full of "baseless and repackaged claims," but it enabled them to seize ballots and other election materials from the 2020 election, which Mr. Trump has repeatedly claimed he won. Federal agents in Fulton County packed up more than 600 boxes of election records. Then director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, watched as boxes of ballots were loaded onto trucks. Barrett has no idea where the ballots are now. She believes the seizure was "political theater aimed at undermining the 2026 and 2028 elections." "I think it was all part of this concerted effort that's happening nationwide to undermine faith in elections," Barrett said. Three months ago, the FBI temporarily reassigned 260 analysts to work on a "priority investigation" into the Georgia materials, according to an internal FBI email obtained by 60 Minutes. So far, nothing has come of the investigation. There have been dozens of probes into the 2020 election in Fulton County, but none have moved the needle. "People see all of these investigations and FBI raids and subpoenas and they say, 'Something must be wrong there. Why should I believe the results?'" The Justice Department responds Dhillon, the head of the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department, said the administration is aggressively pursuing new investigations and they are looking at "thousands" of possible cases of noncitizen voting. "We've been in office for less than two years. We've had investigations ongoing for over a year and it takes time," Dhillon said. Dhillon said there have been irregularities during prior elections, and that a record number of election observers and monitors – more than 1,000 of them – would be at the polls during midterms as a way to increase voter confidence. Recent surveys show that only about half of Americans expect the midterms to be free and fair. Dhillon called concerns that Mr. Trump might challenge midterm results "paranoia." If a noncitizen votes, that individual vote would be challenged, she said, not the entire election. "I don't know what is going to happen," Dhillon told 60 Minutes, "but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states." item.title: Ukraine claims world's first drone evacuation of wounded soldier
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade shared a video on Monday showing an injured soldier evacuated by drone. (Ukraine's 92nd Assault Brigade) Ukraine has shared a video showing what it says is the world’s first evacuation of an injured soldier from the frontlines by drone. The “historic” mission comes just as Kyiv faces a dire turn in its relationship with Washington over the withdrawal of support in its fight against Russia . Shared by the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade on Monday, the video shows the soldier strapping himself into a large drone and being flown at what appears to be relatively low altitude over blurred-out territory. The drone carefully lowers him down and the drone operator greets him with “Welcome back to the ground!” The video also showed blurred faces of drone operators who carried out the mission. The post said the unidentified infantryman was wounded while at his position. “Due to intense enemy drone activity and the presence of landmines, evacuation using conventional unmanned ground vehicles was impossible,” the brigade said. “At that point, the specialists in our unit took it upon themselves to attempt something that had never been done before: evacuating a serviceman using an aerial drone,” it added. The craft used was a heavy-lift hexacopter, it said, originally designed as a bomber by a Ukrainian manufacturer. It looks about twice the size of the soldier in the video. The specialists working on the mission had to ensure the drone could carry a human being without flipping over or swaying excessively, according to the unit. The rescued soldier is currently undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, the brigade added. The squad leader and programmer with the brigade, only identified by his call sign Napalm, called the soldier a “hero” for agreeing to the mission, “having seen and heard the kind of machine that had arrived to get him.” In a separate statement, Ukraine’s Ground Forces said its drone units are already conducting operations “that were recently considered science fiction.” The unidentified infantryman was lifted out in a drone rescue mission after he was wounded at his position. (Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade ) The war has increasingly become a technological arms race, with both Ukraine and Russia relying on drones to reduce human casualties. The conflict has taken a severe toll on both armies, although neither side reports up-to-date numbers of those killed, injured or missing. Ukraine in particular has faced a severe shortage of manpower as it has tried to ramp up recruitment. Ukraine had a major leap in drone technology this year, allowing it to limit Russian logistics in occupied territories as well as strike deeper inside Russia to target Russian oil refineries , commercial warehouses and data centers . Fires at an oil refinery in Moscow, following a reported Ukrainian drone strike, on Sept. 20. (Reuters) “This mission proves once again that Ukrainian service members, working in tandem with Ukrainian manufacturers, are setting global trends in the conduct of warfare,” the brigade’s statement added. Despite hoping that its drone innovation would give it the upper hand at the negotiating table, Kyiv has faced pressure from the U.S. to halt its strikes on Russian oil sites after President Donald Trump signed a diesel deal with the Kremlin earlier this month. Kyiv has since also reported gaps in intelligence sharing and restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is crucial for its drone missions, battlefield communications and air defense. A Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Kyiv on Tuesday. (Genya Savilov/AFP; Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine / via Getty) The drone evacuation comes just days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the Ukrainian government had approved an “experimental project” to use drones for medical logistics. Koretskyi said flights would require coordination with the military, and drones would be given a special status and would be identifiable in the air. “During the war, moving medical cargo by road can cost critical time, especially for transplants,” he said. “Drones will be able to carry medicines, medical products, blood samples, and donor organs between hospitals, including from remote areas.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/world/ukraine/ukraine-first-drone-evacuation-wounded-soldier-frontlines-hexacopter-rcna604310

item.title: Witnesses mistook sounds for gunfire as pickup plowed through Kansas soccer game
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Witnesses of Saturday’s deadly collision in which a pickup truck barreled through a youth soccer game in Kansas, killing two people and injuring nearly a dozen others, said they are haunted by what they saw and heard. Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, were killed in the incident, which unfolded shortly before 3:30 p.m. at the city-owned Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, police said. The deceased were both from McPherson, Kansas, but were not related to each other, a Wichita police spokesperson said. Ten other people, ages 5 to 68, were also hit and hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries, Police Capt. Aaron Moses said. Police said a dark Chevrolet pickup drove onto a field during a youth soccer game and struck children and adults. Erica Case said it was halftime during her 9-year-old son’s soccer game on an adjacent field when she first heard an engine revving, followed by several “boom” sounds. “I saw the truck hitting things. I saw debris flying in the air,” she recalled. “I don’t know if it was a cone, a chair or a person, but you could see matter flying as the truck was barreling through the soccer field at a decent rate of speed.” She said the sound will haunt her. “The moment that I recognized that that wasn’t gunshots, that that was bodies, I lost it,” Case said. “I lost it because it wasn’t just adults. It was also children.” Police were investigating what caused the pickup truck to barrel through a soccer field, killing a man and a child. (David Griekspoor) Case recalled the mother of another boy shouting that she was a nurse and needed to get to the injured. Case said she told her she would watch her boy and then took the woman’s son to safety amid the chaos. It took about 10 minutes for emergency services to arrive, she said, but people began helping the victims during that time. “There are a lot of silent heroes that I know experienced much worse than I did, having to do mouth-to-mouth or CPR on somebody that’d been ran over by a truck,” Case said. David Griekspoor was at the complex with his nephew, who also plays soccer, when he witnessed the incident. “It sounded like small gunfire,” he said. “Bap, bap, bap.” He said it wasn’t clear what was producing the sound until he focused on the truck. “You look up, and you just see the truck going through a line of people,” Griekspoor said. He said his brother and sister-in-law went to check on children nearby as he grabbed his nephew and “backed out of there.” All ended up safe, Griekspoor said. Police said they interviewed more than 30 witnesses. The pickup’s driver, a 34-year-old woman from Garden City, Kansas, was taken into custody but was later released after police consulted with the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office. She has not been charged with a crime and has not been identified. Police said the woman, who had two children in the pickup, had a child who had a soccer game on a different field at the complex. The driver was cooperating with officers, said Moses, the police captain. What caused the pickup to drive through the field was still under investigation, and police said the results of an examination of the vehicle, as well as of toxicology testing on the driver, were pending. item.title: DOJ accuses judge in D.C. golf course case of violating 'basic norms' of impartiality
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A federal judge refused the Department of Justice's (DOJ) demand to step aside from a key hearing on Monday over the future of East Potomac Park, which President Trump wants to renovate into a championship-style golf course. The Trump administration has accused U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes of bias after she yelled at a government attorney last week to express disappointment that hundreds of trees were cut down at the park without additional notice. The DOJ accused her of “violating the basic norms” that a judge be fair and impartial. “It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion. But it is much harder to meet the demanding legal standard against a full record,” Reyes wrote in a 13-page opinion denying the effort late Sunday. “By any objective measure, the Government fails to meet the standard for recusal,” she continued. Reyes, an appointee of former President Biden who serves on the federal bench in the nation’s capital, oversees a lawsuit brought by a preservationist group and individual golfers. They challenge Trump’s desire for a massive renovation at East Potomac Park that would shift it into a championship-style golf course, saying the project is unlawful. The president unveiled a new plan for the site Sunday. “The judge on the case is a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane?” Trump wrote on Truth Social early Monday. The lawsuit has been ongoing for months, but tensions reached a new high after the administration informed the judge on a Friday afternoon that hundreds of trees would be cut down that weekend. The judge has said she’s furious and disappointed with the government for not providing her additional notice before the landscaping, and she has since blocked any additional tree-clearing. The Justice Department in demanding her recusal took issue with the judge’s heated rhetoric — at one point she asked a government lawyer if they were unable to use a phone or drive a car — as well as her demands that Trump administration witnesses show up on a federal holiday to testify before her. “The Government created an emergent situation.
